opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the starting point was that when we saw the early results from the new reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning, it was pretty clear they were getting really good at thinking through hard problems step by step, especially in domains like math and coding where you can check whether the answer is right. And a few of us were thinking, okay, what's a really useful task where that kind of extended reasoning would make a huge difference? Browsing felt like a natural fit.

If you think about how a person does deep research online, you search for something, you read a few pages, you realize the information isn't quite what you need, you refine your query, you follow a link, you backtrack. It's this long, iterative process, and it requires a lot of judgment about what's reliable and what's relevant. That's exactly the type of thing that's hard to hand-engineer but where a model trained end to end with RL can learn the strategy itself.

The other piece was just personal motivation. I think a lot of us were spending hours doing research for things, whether for work or just in our own lives, like comparing products or digging into a topic, and it felt like there was a lot of value in having a model that could go off for, say, five, ten, thirty minutes and come back with a really thorough, well-cited report. So it was a combination of the technical capability finally being there and a really clear use case where people would actually save a lot of time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it came out of frustration with how we were building agents before. I'd worked on earlier browsing efforts, and the way those worked was that you'd take a model that was already trained, write a lot of scaffolding and prompting around it, and try to get it to do something useful on the web. It sort of worked, but it was brittle. The model wasn't actually learning from its mistakes. Every time it hit a page that looked slightly different, or it clicked the wrong thing, it had no mechanism to get better at that, and you'd just be patching around it.

What was exciting about the new RL approach was that it closed that loop. You could give the model a task where there's a verifiable answer at the end, let it browse, let it fail a lot, and have it actually learn which strategies worked. And browsing turned out to be a really natural fit for that, because so much of what makes it hard is sequential. You have to decide what to search for, read a result, realize it's not quite what you need, refine the query, go deeper, back out, cross-reference something else. That's a long chain of decisions, and the early mistakes compound. It's exactly the kind of problem where you want the model to be optimized over the whole trajectory rather than one step at a time.

The other thing is that browsing is a pretty direct test of whether an agent can do real research. If you can ask something a hard question that requires pulling together information from a dozen sources, and it can actually go find them and synthesize an answer you'd trust, that's genuinely useful to people. So it felt like both a good test bed for the method and something that would matter if it worked.

astra-6.text: What interested me was that browsing is a task where you have to make a sequence of decisions. You search for something, look at the results, decide which page to open, and then work out whether you have enough information or need to keep going. That seemed like a natural fit for reinforcement learning: could the model learn better ways to navigate that process from feedback on whether it ultimately answered the question? And it’s a useful capability—there are so many questions where answering well requires going out and finding information.

sol-6.1.text: What interested me was that browsing is a very natural setting for learning through trial and error. You take an action, see what happens, and decide what to do next. And a lot of tasks have a concrete outcome: did you find the information, or did you complete what the user asked for? That makes it an interesting place to explore whether reinforcement learning can help a model go beyond answering questions and actually carry out tasks over multiple steps.
